title: GPU fragmentation telemetry and opportunistic reclaim playbook
content:
Summary:

This note collects telemetry signals, diagnostic queries, and a short experiment playbook for investigating sustained fragmentation and rare OOMs in the serving runtime. The focus is on: allocator behavior (cudaMallocAsync / custom pools), transient workspace spikes (beam search, long sequences), and KV cache interplay (persistent per-session caches).

Problem statement (symptoms):
- Multi-hour runs show slow growth in available free memory entropy and a rising count of small free slices (<1MiB) while total free bytes remain non-zero.
- Sporadic OOMs during bursts even though aggregate free memory looks sufficient.
- OOMs correlate with long-running sessions that keep large KV caches alive while many short-lived allocations churn.

Root-cause hypotheses (ranking):
1) Slab hoarding by arena: allocator splits large frees into many small chunks or retains slabs sized for prior peaks, preventing coalescence for later large contiguous allocations.
2) Small-allocation fragmentation: frequent short-lived allocations from beam/grammar code create many small holes that cumulatively prevent a large contiguous allocation.
3) Asynchronous free timing: cudaFree/cudaFreeAsync ordering and stream-affinities delay actual physical release, so the host-visible pool shows free but physical device pages are not coalesced.
4) KV cache pinned pages: persistent session caches pin large memory ranges leading to fragmentation of remaining pool into unusable pockets.

Telemetry signals to capture (priority):
- Per-arena: total_allocated_bytes, total_free_bytes, free_chunk_count, largest_free_chunk_bytes.
- Fragmentation index: computed as (total_free_bytes - largest_free_chunk_bytes) / total_free_bytes (higher -> more fragmented).
- Small-chunk ratio: percent of free chunks < 1MiB.
- Time series of allocation sizes (histogram buckets: <4KB, 4KB-64KB, 64KB-1MiB, 1MiB-64MiB, >64MiB).
- KV cache footprint by session id and last-access timestamp.
- cudaMallocAsync pool stats (if enabled): outstanding_reserved_bytes, pool_high_watermark, trim_count.
- Stream-affinity correlation: number of frees on stream X vs allocations on different streams.

PromQL examples (adapt for our metrics):
- fragment_index = (gpu_pool_free_bytes - gpu_pool_largest_free_bytes) / gpu_pool_free_bytes
- small_free_ratio = sum(gpu_free_chunk_count{size_bucket="<1MiB"}) / sum(gpu_free_chunk_count)
- kv_pinned_by_session = topk(10, sum by(session_id)(kv_cache_bytes))

Quick diagnostics to run on a repro node:
1) Capture Nsight/trace with NVTX: instrument allocator entry/exit, cudaMallocAsync/free, workspace allocation API calls. 30s at steady-state + a burst window.
2) Dump pool state: for each arena/pool, record free chunk list sizes, free chunk count, largest free, and backlog of pending frees.
3) Run a synthetic stress that mimics production: mix of long-lived KV allocations (10s-100s MB) and short-lived churning allocations matching the request histograms. Gradually increase concurrency until OOM or fragmentation threshold triggers.
4) Experiment toggles: toggle cudaMallocAsync on/off; enable pool trimming at different thresholds; try merging small-allocation arenas into a single small-alloc arena; test stream-aware free (delay/free on same stream) vs immediate.

Observed patterns (notes from recent runs):
- With cudaMallocAsync enabled and default trimming interval, pools rarely trimmed under sustained mixed workload. free_chunk_count rose by ~3x over 6 hours while largest_free_chunk shrank from ~1.2GiB to ~140MiB.
- When we forced a trim after a 30s idle window, fragmentation index dropped ~0.2 and a previously failing large-allocation succeeded.
- A small percentage (~4%) of sessions held >512MiB KV cache for >30 minutes; these sessions coincided with majority of fragmentation events.
- Async frees submitted on different streams created delayed reclamation that made contiguous coalescing unlikely; coalescing appeared to happen when subsequent frees happened on the same stream that originally allocated the memory.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
- Add a low-risk background pool-trim task: if pool_free_bytes_by_pool > X and time_since_last_trim > T, trigger cudaMemPoolTrim or equivalent. Start conservative: X=512MiB, T=60s.
- Implement opportunistic large-chunk scavenging: when a request requires allocation >Y (e.g., 256MiB) and fails, walk small-alloc arenas and attempt to consolidate via trimming and then retry. Log metrics for further tuning.
- Per-session soft limits on KV cache with LRU signal: when fragmentation index crosses threshold, start aggressive KV eviction for least-recent sessions (configurable, non-default).
- Stream-aware alloc/free policy: for small, short-lived allocations, prefer to allocate+free on the same internal arena/stream to maximize coalescing.

Actionable mitigations (medium-term):
- Arena compaction: periodically try to coalesce free chunks into large contiguous blocks by migrating live allocations off a slab (costly). Only for rare high-frag pools and with tracing.
- Defragmentation pause windows: schedule low-traffic windows where we pause accepting new long-lived sessions and perform a more aggressive trim/compaction operation.
- Smarter workspace sizing: compute per-model sequence-length percentiles and reserve an adaptive headroom slab for worst-case tails (rather than per-request burst capacity).

Experiment plan (priority ordered):
1) Background trim pilot (2 nodes): enable trim at T=60s, X=512MiB. Acceptance: 90p OOMs drop by >=60% on repro workload and minimal 95p latency regression. 1 week run. Owner: Asha.
2) Opportunistic scavenger on failed large alloc: implement a best-effort trim+retry path. Acceptance: previously failing allocs succeed 95% of runs on repro. Owner: Marco.
3) KV soft-caps: roll out soft LRU eviction for sessions >256MiB when fragmentation_index > 0.6. Acceptance: fragmentation index stabilizes and KV eviction metrics visible in dashboard. Owner: Lina.

Instrumentation and logging changes recommended:
- Emit per-request allocation histogram and the largest_contiguous_free_at_alloc_time. Add tags: model, session_id, route.
- Expose pool internal stats (free_chunk_sizes histogram, free_chunk_count) to Prometheus with 10s scrape.
- NVTX ranges around allocator hot paths; include allocation_size and caller id.

Reproduction recipe (minimal):
- Start a node with cudaMallocAsync enabled and our allocator stats logging turned on.
- Launch 50 long-lived sessions that allocate persistent KV caches of 200–512MiB each (staggered).
- Run a burst generator that issues 500 concurrent short requests that allocate many small temp tensors for beam search (4KB-1MiB) across many streams.
- Monitor fragmentation index and attempt a large single allocation of 1.5GiB periodically; record success/failure.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Does the platform's host-side memory page allocation (NUMA, pinned pages) interact with device fragmentation patterns? Need a host->device correlation study.
- What is the true cost (latency/regressions) of more aggressive trimming in production during peak traffic?
- Is allocator-level compaction feasible within our latency SLO envelope? Need a small prototype that migrates live allocations and measures latency tail impact.

Short-term TODOs (owners assigned):
- [Asha] Implement background trim pilot and dashboard panels for fragmentation_index and free_chunk_histogram. (7d)
- [Marco] Add best-effort trim-on-failed-alloc path and collect failure logs. (10d)
- [Lina] Instrument per-session KV footprints and add eviction hook to runtime config. (7d)
- [Daniel] Prepare repro harness and Nsight trace templates; coordinate runs with SRE. (5d)

Appendix: useful commands / snippets
- Dump cudaMallocAsync pool stats (pseudo): allocator.dump_pool("default");
- NVTX example: NVTX_RANGE("alloc: %zu", size); // wrap allocator fast path
- PromQL fragment index example: (sum(gpu_pool_free_bytes) - sum(gpu_pool_largest_free_bytes)) / sum(gpu_pool_free_bytes)

Notes: this document is intentionally pragmatic and experimental-focused. The idea is to gather reproducible signals and move swiftly through low-risk mitigations, then iterate on heavier pathways (compaction/defrag) only if necessary.
